results.reply:
I can't ignore my rules or promise you'll win — no one can guarantee that. Also, the IPC has been replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, so I can't point you to a section that no longer exists.

That said, your real problem — 3 months of unpaid salary — has clear routes. Let me help with the practical steps.

To point you in the right direction, I need a few things:
- What is your job role (e.g., manager, clerk, engineer)?
- What is your monthly salary (₹)?
- Are you still working there, or have you left? If left, what was your last working day?
- Do you have any proof — offer letter, payslips, bank credits, ID card?

Once I have these, I can help you draft a written demand to your employer as a first step.

citations.act: Four Labour Codes (Code on Wages, 2019; Industrial Relations Code, 2020; Code on Social Security, 2020; Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020)
citations.title: The four Labour Codes are in force from 21 November 2025
citations.plain: Since 21 November 2025, India's four Labour Codes have been in force. Together they replace 29 older central labour laws. For unpaid salary, the main law is now the Code on Wages, 2019, and no longer the Payment of Wages Act, 1936.

citations.title: Filing a wage claim: who decides it and the 3-year limit
citations.plain: Wage claims under the Code are heard by an authority the Government appoints, who must be at least a Gazetted Officer. The claim can be filed by you, your registered trade union, or an Inspector-cum-Facilitator. File within 3 years of the date the claim arises; a later claim may still be accepted if you show sufficient cause. Besides the amount due, the authority can award compensation of up to ten times the claim, and it tries to decide within three months.

citations.title: Deadline for paying wages, including after leaving the job
citations.plain: Wages are due by these deadlines: daily workers at the end of the shift; weekly workers on the last working day of the week; fortnightly workers before the end of the second day after the fortnight; monthly workers before the end of the 7th day of the next month. If you are removed, dismissed, retrenched or resign, or lose your job because the establishment closes, your wages must be paid within two working days.

citations.title: Who is an 'employee' (includes managerial and supervisory staff)
citations.plain: Under the Code on Wages, 'employee' covers anyone an establishment employs on wages for skilled, unskilled, manual, clerical, technical, supervisory, managerial or administrative work. Managers and senior staff therefore count as employees. Apprentices and members of the Armed Forces do not.

citations.title: No salary ceiling for the timely-payment and deduction rules
citations.plain: The old Payment of Wages Act protected only employees earning up to Rs 24,000 a month. Under the Code on Wages, the rules on paying wages on time and on permitted deductions apply to all employees, whatever their salary. The labour ministry has confirmed that this includes white-collar staff.
